report: Monday, 16 November. The facts here come from the earlier review today. The chip selloff resumed before Nvidia results this week. Nasdaq futures were down about one percent. Copper sat at a four-month low. A reported Iranian strike on a US base in Bahrain had only one source, and Brent rose only about half a percent. The trader placed no orders today. It kept Infineon, because the record quarter and the guidance of more than 20 percent growth still stand. It did not buy oil, Bayer or anything else, because no catalyst was confirmed by a primary source. So there were no orders, no fills and no costs today. One position is open: six Infineon shares bought at 50.90, now 49.24. That is about 9.90 euros down on paper. The stop is near 46.82, about 5 percent below today's price. The exit date is 24 November, six trading days away. Day result: minus 3.82 euros, or minus 0.19 percent. Equity is 1987.56 euros, minus 0.62 percent since the 2000 euro start. Reconcile is consistent and there are no warnings. Odd points: this is a second review for the same day, and the input brings no new news beyond the earlier handoff. One small losing day on one stock says nothing about skill. No trade has closed and no shadow call has scored yet, so there is nothing to learn from yet.
questions: Infineon is held through Nvidia results with a stop about 8 percent below entry and a 10-day exit. Should the rules say anything about holding a position through a big outside event like that, or is the stop enough?

This is the second review on the same decision day, and the earlier run worked with Infineon quotes about 62 hours old. Should the pipeline block duplicate runs and mark stale quotes more clearly before the trader decides?

The trader only buys when the expected move is well above twice the entry cost. With about 1692 euros in cash and small position sizes, what does a round trip actually cost in percent, and is twice the cost the right bar?
